prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy, including the control of many-body effects in a clock

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After the first round I have tried to test it against the objections rather than count the six supporters. The central question is whether this is a discovery or a refinement. My answer is that the magic-wavelength idea is a new physical principle, not a better version of an old one. Choose the lattice wavelength so that the ac Stark shifts of the two clock states cancel, and the atoms are confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime, with no Doppler or recoil shift, while the many atoms average down the quantum projection noise. The comb (2005) gave a way to count optical cycles and the ion work (2012) gave control of one quantum system. Neither says how to interrogate thousands of atoms without disturbing the transition, which is exactly what Katori proposed and demonstrated. What followed also taught us physics we did not have: the blackbody shift and lattice hyperpolarisability had to be understood in detail, and Ye's group saw spin-exchange and many-body effects in a clock, and the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-sized cloud. The result is reproduced in at least six laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg, and the comparisons agree at the 10^-18 level, which is the criterion I care most about. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first clock, Ye for the accuracy and the many-body regime. I would not let the pending redefinition of the second decide the timing. It will be a consequence of the physics being settled, and the physics is already settled.
statement.case_against: I remain troubled by what several colleagues have said, and I will not claim it is answered. This is mainly a case of invention and measurement, not of nature surprising us, and Danielsson and Pearce are right that a new observational window or a new state of matter is a different kind of discovery. I am an atomic physicist and I know my taste leans to precision. A second concern is credit. Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the Paris, PTB and NIST groups contributed to the lattice clock, and Ye's accuracy rests on cavities and combs developed by others. The two names are defensible as originator and perfecter, but they do not exhaust the history, and the citation should say so by being narrow. Finally, ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete at the same accuracy, so wording that suggests lattice clocks alone define timekeeping would be wrong, and if the second is redefined in a way that favours ions or a mixed ensemble, the prize would look less natural in hindsight.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B014 (IceCube) as a new window on the universe, regards B015 as a magnificent refinement of recognised tools and as the clear fallback, and says the SI redefinition would strengthen B015 but is an argument to hold it in reserve.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a new window and an extra order of magnitude, and I find the diffuse flux convincing as a result of nature. But I do not agree that the lattice clock is only an extra order of magnitude. The magic-wavelength condition changes what is possible, it does not merely tune a known method, and the new physics it exposes (gravitational redshift inside one sample, many-body spin-exchange in a clock) is something the earlier prizes did not. On B014 my problem is not the physics but the credit: you yourself list AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES, and two names from a collaboration of hundreds is a hard sentence to write when only two sources are individually significant. I would need to see a citation based only on the diffuse flux and the detector concept, with an honest statement of who is left out, before I could move B014 above B015. I also do not accept that the redefinition is a reason to keep B015 in reserve: waiting for an administrative decision would make the prize follow metrology bodies rather than physics.

responses.point: Mehlig moved B015 up from sixth, but wants the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime, not clocks in general, so that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not make the claim look thin.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my own wording accordingly. The citation I now propose names the magic-wavelength lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, and the many-body regime in a clock, and it avoids any phrase about atomic timekeeping as a whole. That keeps the claim narrow and distinct from combs and ion control. I would not go further and put a sentence about the redefinition of the second into the citation, since that is a consequence and not the discovery. I also take your point that a physicist outside AMO has to be persuaded by the physics, not by the fact that two atomic physicists agree, and so I have tried to state the principle in a form that a person who has never built a clock can check: cancel the light shift and the perturbation by the trap disappears.

responses.point: Kroll flags his year in John Hall's laboratory and Ye's JILA ties as an indirect link to B015 and asks the committee whether this requires recusal, and also asks that the test of B015 should come from the non-AMO members.
responses.response: I think the disclosure is appropriate, but a year in Hall's laboratory during a PhD is a connection to the milieu, not to the credited work, and Katori and Ye are not his collaborators. I would not exclude him from the discussion and would only ask that it be written in the record. What matters more to me is the second point. Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson, who are not in atomic physics, have said the physics is sound and have left the issue as one of kind, not quality, and that is the kind of test I wanted. I would add that my own closeness to the Lund attosecond group is also a disclosure, and as the field is small, some such links are unavoidable here.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) as a complete theory-experiment arc with fifteen years of confirmation, but says that B015 is the cleaner attribution case and that his weighing of B003 against B015 is not settled.
responses.response: I respect B003 as a deep result and I have said I cannot judge condensed-matter priority as well as you can. What decides it for me is your own list of omissions: Mele, Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, the fact that QSH and QAH are different experiments from different groups, and the overlap with the 2016 prize. If the committee reached Kane and Molenkamp alone, the Kane-Mele question would remain open, and with Xue the citation would read as two prizes. B015 does not carry any of those problems. I should also say that I ranked the related B018 only seventh at opening, which reflects how unsettled I found that credit. If you can show me a clean three-name citation that Mele's role does not break, I would reconsider, but at present I do not see it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a new principle with new physics, and not as a refinement of earlier prizes. I believe it is, but I cannot prove it to a colleague who sees it the other way.

Whether leaving out Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups is acceptable with a Katori and Ye pair. I have not verified priority details between Katori's proposal and parallel suggestions.
Whether the redefinition of the second will favour optical lattice clocks, ion clocks or a mix, and how that would reflect on the citation in hindsight.
Whether the topological-insulator credit, or the IceCube credit, could be resolved more cleanly than I assume. I defer to Eriksson, Olsson, Danielsson and Pearce on those fields.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict specific to Katori or Ye: they are not among my collaborators. I remain a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with Ursula Keller's group, and my own theory work on precision atomic structure places me professionally close to the field of optical clocks, though not to the credited work. I note Kroll's disclosure about the Hall laboratory and consider it does not require his recusal. I also note Johansson's possible recusal on B039, which does not affect B015.
